articles.body: El Comité Organizador de los Juegos Olímpicos y Paralímpicos de Los Ángeles 2028 anunció este miércoles que el eslogan oficial de la competición será 'Las estrellas se alinean' ('Stars Align'). El lema oficial fue presentado con un vídeo ambientado con la música de Red Hot Chili Peppers que combina hazañas de otros eventos deportivos con planos que reflejan el estilo de la vida y la iconografía de la ciudad californiana. Entre ellos, el emblemático Memorial Coliseum de Los Ángeles que acogerá la ceremonia de inauguración de los Juegos junto al estadio SoFi de Inglewood. Será la primera vez en la historia olímpica que la apertura se celebre en dos sedes a la vez. "Los Ángeles es el lugar donde los sueños se hacen realidad, y los Juegos Olímpicos nos muestran lo que es posible cuando el mundo se une", aseguró Casey Wasserman, presidente de LA28, en un comunicado. Según explicó, el eslogan hace referencia a la asociación de Los Ángeles, conocida popularmente como la Ciudad de los Sueños, con el entretenimiento, la cultura y la creatividad: "Cuando el triunfo del deporte se encuentra con la ciudad de los sueños, 'Las estrellas se alinean'". "Estamos deseando que las estrellas se alineen en 2028 para poder compartir este momento con todos", añadió Wasserman. La organización también busca convertir el eslogan en "un grito de guerra" para los atletas que compitan durante los Juegos, para los voluntarios que presenten su ayuda y para los aficionados que acudan a la cita. Los Juegos Olímpicos de Los Ángeles se inaugurarán el 14 de julio de 2028, seguidos de los Juegos Paralímpicos, que lo harán el 15 de agosto.

articles.title: Hyrox partners with World Triathlon in bid to become Olympic sport
articles.summary: Hyrox moves closer to its "ultimate ambition" of gaining Olympic and Paralympic status after entering into a partnership with World Triathlon.
articles.body:
Hyrox has moved closer to fulfilling its ambition of gaining inclusion into the Olympic and Paralympic Games after entering into a partnership with World Triathlon.

The agreement will see 'hybrid racing' become a recognised discipline within World Triathlon, the sport's global governing body.

Hyrox, the fitness craze which combines running with exercise stations, will be contested across three formats - ultimate, fast and ultra - each sanctioned and governed by World Triathlon.

World Triathlon and Hyrox said in a statement that obtaining Olympic and Paralympic status for the discipline was the "ultimate ambition".

World Triathlon president Antonio Arimany said hybrid racing was "a natural evolution for our movement".

He added: "This partnership will not only accelerate the growth of World Triathlon on the global stage, it will open genuine new opportunities for every one of our national federations to grow participation, engage new audiences, and strengthen our sport at every level.

"This is exactly the kind of forward-looking collaboration our members deserve."

Hyrox co-founder Christian Toetzke said: "From the very beginning, our goal was to build a global sport that could earn a place on the world's biggest athletic stage.

"Partnering with World Triathlon is a monumental step toward that vision.

"Hybrid racing is no longer just a global fitness movement, it is officially on the road to the Olympics."

Great Britain's Olympic triathlon champion Alex Yee reacted to the news by sharing a poll with his 227,000 followers, who had voted 82% against being in favour of the move after a couple of hours.

Fellow British triathlete Max Stapley commented on the joint announcement on Instagram: "This is crap."

Olympic triathlete Roksana Slupek, of Poland, wrote "the two sports have absolutely nothing in common" and questioned what her sport would gain from the partnership.

How Hyrox became the latest sporting craze

Hyrox apologises for allowing race to continue after athlete soils herself

Hyrox was founded in 2017, primarily as an indoor discipline in which athletes take part in eight legs consisting of a one-kilometre run followed by a fitness exercise.

The exercises include 1km on a standing ski machine, 50m sled push, 50m sled pull, 80m burpee jumps, 1km row, 200m kettlebell carry, 100m lunges carrying a sandbag, and 100 throws and catches of a medicine ball against a wall.

World championships are held each year, with athletes contesting both singles and doubles races.

Under the agreement with World Triathlon, Hyrox will continue to oversee world, continental and national championships for elite athletes in the 'ultimate' format, which mirrors its existing format.

The additional formats included under the new discipline of hybrid racing - 'fast' and 'ultra' - offer high intensity and extended adaptations.

Only sports governed by recognised international federations which comply with the Olympic Charter, the World Anti-Doping Code and the Olympic Movement Code on the Prevention of the Manipulation of Competition - as is the case for triathlon - are eligible for inclusion at the Olympic and Paralympic Games.

articles.title: El Atlètic Barceloneta tritura al Jadran Split y sigue invicto
articles.standfirst: El equipo no pierde un partido europeo desde el 29 de octubre de 2025
articles.summary: El equipo no pierde un partido europeo desde el 29 de octubre de 2025
articles.body: El Zodiac Atlètic Barceloneta, vigente campeón de Europa, trituró este miércoles al Jadran Split croata (7-17) con una gran segunda mitad, en la que firmó un parcial de 2-9, para prolongar su pleno de victorias en la primera fase de la Liga de Campeones. El triunfo incontestable del equipo que dirige Fran Fernández le permite mantener su brillante racha continental, ya que no pierde un partido europeo desde el 29 de octubre de 2025, cuando cayó ante el Marsella. El conjunto marinero no dio opción a su rival y tomó pronto el control del encuentro con un parcial inicial de 1-4 que encarriló la victoria. El Jadran reaccionó en el segundo cuarto, en el que igualó el parcial (4-4), pero tras el descanso el Atlètic Barceloneta volvió a imponer su superioridad. Vince Vigvari, con cinco goles, y Unai Biel y Bernat Sanahuja, con tres cada uno, lideraron el ataque visitante en una segunda mitad en la que el conjunto barcelonés desarboló al equipo croata. También destacó Unai Aguirre, que firmó diez paradas, en un encuentro en el que el Atlètic Barceloneta mostró además una notable eficacia en las superioridades numéricas, con siete goles en once ocasiones (7/11). El 7-17 definitivo permite al vigente campeón continuar al frente del grupo C.

articles.title: IA española para revolucionar los Juegos Olímpicos
articles.standfirst: El riojano Alejandro Merino-Madrid lidera el proyecto encaminado en distintas líneas: evitar el ciberacoso a los deportistas, captar talento, optimizar recursos, ayudar a los jueces en decisiones...
articles.summary: El riojano Alejandro Merino-Madrid lidera el proyecto encaminado en distintas líneas: evitar el ciberacoso a los deportistas, captar talento, optimizar recursos, ayudar a los jueces en decisiones...
articles.body: Un patinador que inicia un salto con 30 grados de desviación. El meñique de un gimnasta que pisa fuera del tapiz. Un mensaje de odio dirigido a un atleta a las tres de la mañana. Son situaciones que el ojo humano tarda en ver o que nadie atiende a tiempo, y el Comité Olímpico Internacional (COI) cree que la inteligencia artificial puede resolverlas. Quien lidera esa apuesta es un ingeniero aeroespacial de Logroño: Alejandro Merino, de 39 años, cuyo rictus muestra la ilusión del que aspira a una medalla de oro en unos Juegos Olímpicos mientras expone el tema. Merino llegó al COI en 2024, tras unas 13 entrevistas, para dirigir la Agenda Olímpica de IA. Su currículum explica el salto: empezó en 2010 en la empresa GMV con un proyecto de "diseño guiado por datos" para Airbus, antes de que existiera ChatGPT y que las dos palabras que más se han pronunciado en los últimos tiempos se uniesen para nombrar la Inteligencia Artificial. Desde entonces ha pasado por los sectores aeronáutico, aeroespacial, de automoción y de semiconductores. "Mi trabajo consiste en preparar al movimiento olímpico para la llegada de la inteligencia artificial: mitigar los riesgos, aprovechar las oportunidades y conseguir que la IA apoye a los atletas y al deporte", resume delante de un té. Una de las herramientas más sensibles es la que protege a los deportistas del ciberacoso. "Estamos desarrollando una especie de centinela, como un vigilante, que observa lo que ocurre en las redes sociales", explica. "No se trata de censurar la crítica deportiva", aclara. "Decir que a alguien no le gusta cómo corre es libertad de expresión. Otra cosa son los mensajes racistas, machistas o los deseos de muerte". El sistema relaciona el contenido denunciado con la norma concreta que infringe en cada plataforma, para que X o TikTok no puedan despachar el caso como un asunto de opinión. "Si el proceso funciona bien, el contenido puede retirarse en cuestión de minutos y la campaña de odio se detiene antes de que avance. Se le transmite a la plataforma que ese mensaje vulnera su artículo tal y la eliminan", señala. De 2,4 millones de interacciones examinadas entre los olímpicos de invierno de este año, 10.200 resultaron ser mensajes de odio. Para Los Ángeles dentro de dos años, el COI quiere ampliar la aplicación que ya usan los deportistas en la Villa Olímpica, hoy limitada a información práctica como dónde están la cafetería y la lavandería. La idea es que puedan preguntarle cualquier duda, incluso si alguien les ofrece dinero para dejarse ganar. Muchos atletas que no son estrellas no tienen un entrenador dedicado en exclusiva, y la IA les daría ese "primer nivel de orientación". Algo parecido ocurre con NOCnet, la red de los 206 comités olímpicos nacionales. Si un comité quiere saber cómo tramitar la beca de una campeona olímpica, ya no depende del horario de Suiza: "Alguien al otro lado del mundo puede preguntar a las tres de la mañana en Suiza y hacerlo en el idioma que prefiera, dentro de los que se manejan en el COI". Durante los Juegos de Invierno de Milán-Cortina, la app de Olympics.com incorporó un asistente de texto para que el aficionado preguntara cosas como "Estoy viendo curling y no entiendo nada. ¿Qué acaba de pasar?". Merino cuenta un fenómeno curioso: al principio las dudas eran básicas, como si la piedra era una pelota o como se llamaba el stick de hockey. Pasadas un par de semanas, las preguntas del conjunto de usuarios ya hablaban de estrategia y táctica. "No analizábamos a cada usuario, solo el cambio en las consultas agregadas", aclara. La gran pregunta es si la IA acabará arbitrando. Merino es prudente: el COI no pretende decir a las federaciones cómo juzgar, y no hay una solución universal. "Hay que estudiarlo deporte por deporte". En patinaje artístico, los jueces de Milán-Cortina, en febrero pasado, contaron con una herramienta desarrollada con Omega que podía detectar, por ejemplo, una desviación de unos 30 grados al iniciar un salto, algo difícil de apreciar sin repeticiones. Con la expresión artística, en cambio, hay que andar con cuidado. Para los Juegos de verano se estudian soluciones como que en gimnasia se pueda comprobar si la punta del pie ha pisado fuera del tapiz. "En lugar de que el árbitro tenga que revisar seis repeticiones y ralentizar el proceso, la herramienta podría señalar la cámara y el instante exactos en los que se produce la infracción. Después, el árbitro tomaría la decisión, por supuesto", describe. La filosofía de cara a 2028 es clara: "La prioridad es que cada vez haya menos subjetividad en aquellos aspectos que se pueden medir de manera objetiva". Muchas federaciones, añade, quieren que los árbitros sigan teniendo un papel central, porque todavía no confían plenamente en la IA. También se comparten soluciones de salud, como medidores de aceleración que alertan de una posible conmoción tras un golpe, en deportes como el rugby. El proyecto que más ha sorprendido a Merino nació en torno a los Juegos Olímpicos de la Juventud de Dakar, que comienza el próximo sábado. Un equipo del movimiento olímpico viajó a Senegal con varias tabletas para ofrecer a más de mil jóvenes con talento pero pocas oportunidades unas pruebas voluntarias: saltos laterales, flexiones, un esprint. La tableta analizaba velocidad de reacción, fuerza y equilibrio para sugerir disciplinas con potencial. "Alguien podía encajar en la lucha libre, otro en el fútbol..". "A veces, en el deporte se dice que hay jóvenes que son ricos sin saberlo", recuerda. Los resultados individuales se entregan a los propios jóvenes, y los agregados, al comité nacional, que puede decidir en qué instalaciones invertir, por ejemplo. El mayor obstáculo aquí es legal. "Almacenar datos de niños y adolescentes de otro país es un asunto muy delicado". India, por ejemplo, limita dónde pueden guardarse los datos y qué proveedores pueden gestionarlos. La IA también llega a la trastienda con el objetivo de reducir costes. Para los medios audiovisuales, el COI crea réplicas digitales de los estadios, con las que se simulan la posición del sol o de las cámaras (el vóley playa con la Torre Eiffel de fondo en París 2024). Con esa réplica, "el equipo audiovisual obtiene el 99 % de la solución antes de desplazarse. Basta enviar a una persona un día, en vez de a todo un equipo tres semanas", expone Merino-Madrid. Además, dentro del propio COI, una herramienta desarrollada con un gran proveedor tecnológico ahorra de media 72 minutos diarios a cada empleado que la usa, según sus mediciones. "El objetivo no es despedir a nadie", subraya Merino, sino liberar tiempo para otras tareas. También a los patrocinadores se les da herramientas para que sus marcas se adapten a las estrictas reglas del manejo de los símbolos olímpicos. Son sólo, en fin, una parte de las posibilidades que da la IA, un agente que marca un futuro distinto para todos.

articles.title: La atleta Julieta Gallego muere en el accidente de tren de Urda
articles.standfirst: De 24 años, era velocista y saltadora de longitud y perteneciente a la AD Sprint
articles.summary: De 24 años, era velocista y saltadora de longitud y perteneciente a la AD Sprint
articles.body: El mundo del deporte y en concreto el del atletismo ha sido físicamente golpeado por la tragedia del accidente ferroviario de Urda. Según informa ABC, entre las víctimas se encuentra la saltadora de longitud Julieta Gallego, de 24 años y perteneciente al club AD Sprint de Madrid. Julieta, especialista en longitud y 60 metros, acreditó una marca de 5,90 metros en longitud en el Campeonato de España por clubes. El presidente de la Real Federación Española de Atletismo, Raúl Chapado, expresó sus condolencias en declaraciones a ABC: "el deporte llora la marcha de Julieta, una vida por delante que se apaga injustamente. El atletismo español abraza el alma de Julieta y el dolor inmenso de su familia, sus amigos y su club de siempre. No están solos en este vacío". La Federación Española transmitió a través de sus redes sociales sus condolencias por el trágico suceso: "Desde la Real Federación Española de Atletismo nos sumamos al dolor y la conmoción por el trágico suceso ferroviario ocurrido en Toledo. Todo nuestro cariño y solidaridad con las familias y seres queridos de las víctimas, y nuestro apoyo a todas las personas afectadas en estos momentos de dolor".

articles.title: Olympic Games: South Africa bids to make Durban host city for 2036 or 2040
articles.summary: South Africa names Durban as host city for its 2036 and 2040 bids to bring the Olympics to Africa for the first time.
articles.body:
Durban is South Africa’s preferred candidate to host the first Olympics in Africa.

South Africa is bidding to host the 2036 or 2040 Summer Olympics and Paralympics. The International Olympic Committee will choose the host city for 2036 in mid-2029.

The country’s choice to put forward Durban, South Africa’s third-biggest city, was announced by the acting president of the South African Sports Confederation, Olympic and Paralympic Committee, Lwandile Simelane, on Thursday. She said Durban would be the main candidate city for South Africa’s bid, but it would likely be a “multi-city bid” that would propose a number of events to be held in other cities.

South Africa’s economic hubs of Johannesburg and Cape Town were also considered as candidate cities.

Durban, a city of about 4 million on the subtropical Indian Ocean coast, was touted as a possible Olympic host city more than a decade ago following South Africa’s staging of the 2010 football World Cup, the first in Africa. But an official bid did not materialise then, largely due to concerns over costs.

The city was stripped of hosting the 2022 Commonwealth Games because it could not make financial or other guarantees required for that event.

Officials said on Thursday they were not yet able to provide any estimates of the cost to South Africa of staging the Olympics if its bid were successful. They said Durban’s bid would be centred on the 56,000-seat Moses Mabhida Stadium, which was built for the 2010 World Cup.

South Africa is among seven countries bidding for the 2036 Games. The others are India , Qatar, South Korea, Germany , Hungary and Turkiye.

The IOC gave October 31 as the deadline for national Olympic committees to formally declare their interest in bidding for the 2036 Games.

Candidates have an opportunity to make virtual presentations to the IOC next month to start the official bidding process. A key date is in March, the IOC has said, when its board will approve a shortlist of candidates.

If it wins, South Africa would be the first African host of the Summer Games since the modern Olympics was created in 1896. Africa’s biggest economy previously failed with a bid to stage the 2004 Games in Cape Town.

The Youth Olympics open this weekend in Dakar, Senegal, marking the first Olympic sports event to be held in Africa.

articles.title: ‘The Pat McAfee Hate Is Ridiculous,’ ‘Bringing Joy to Millions’ — Fans Send ESPN Star Heartfelt Messages After Emotional Statement on Utah Controversy
articles.summary: Pat McAfee has spent years turning sports into a loud, irreverent celebration, but the ESPN personality says the darker side of public attention has become d...
articles.body:
Pat McAfee has spent years turning sports into a loud, irreverent celebration, but the ESPN personality says the darker side of public attention has become difficult to ignore.

Amid the fallout from his University of Utah controversy, McAfee shared screenshots of threatening messages and revealed that he had been avoiding his social media mentions and direct messages because of the abuse.

His emotional statement prompted an outpouring of support, with fans reminding McAfee that the joy he brings to sports still matters to millions.

Pat McAfee Opens Up About Threats Against Him and His Family

On Wednesday, McAfee posted screenshots of threatening messages he said he had received online, including one from a man in Ohio. He admitted that he had deliberately avoided his mentions and direct messages amid the ongoing controversies.

"I've stayed away from my mentions and DM's this month since these back to back days but.. I'm sure if I went in there now, I'd find some wishes for and threats of death for me," McAfee wrote.

The ESPN personality also reflected on the heightened security surrounding a College GameDay broadcast in Tennessee last year. He noted that the FBI, Disney security, Tennessee State Police, Knoxville Police and university authorities coordinated security measures while recalling that security personnel discussed the possibility of him wearing a bulletproof vest.

McAfee also revisited the backlash over his 2024 comments about Algerian Olympic champion Imane Khelif. His original segment included inaccurate claims about Khelif's gender, although McAfee argued Wednesday that subsequent coverage failed to reflect the empathy he also tried to express during the discussion.

Since then, he said, mistakes, missteps and misquotes have repeatedly reignited backlash against him.

"I'm trying my best in real time but.. I am to talk about sports and care about the future of sports," McAfee added. "I owe everything to sports. I'm grateful as hell to do what I do."

"I literally try to love every minute of the incredible opportunities I get to experience but.. it's certainly all a much different life than I could've ever expected. I try to give everything I have, all the time.. I am very sorry to those that despise me."

McAfee's emotional statement prompted an outpouring of support from fans.

"Thanks for getting me through my work days for the PAST 6 YEARS PAT! I still sing the Chris Rice intro sometimes when I'm feeling down. THANK YEW TO YOU AND THE BOYS!!! A lot of us love you brother and I can't imagine what you must feel with these things going on," one said.

"THE PAT MCAFEE HATE IS RIDICULOUS. PAT IS ONE OF THE GOOD GUYS. Pat spends his days spreading positivity and bringing people together through sports. His mantra has always been: 'Be a friend, tell a friend something nice. It might change your life. PatMcAfeeShow does not deserve death threats or attacks on his family and name," ML Football wrote .

McAfee joined College GameDay in 2022 before launching his daily ESPN program in 2023. The college football show's viewership figures reflect its continued popularity, with an average of 2.8 million viewers through Week 7. Its Week 8 broadcast from Utah averaged 2.5 million viewers, with the final hour attracting 3.1 million.

Those figures show that College GameDay continues to draw a substantial audience amid the controversy.

"Keep doing you bud. Y'all are bringing joy to millions and millions of people each week," one said.

"Love Yew brother. Will always support the McAfee Mafia. Chuck those marks. 'Be a friend tell a friend something nice, it might change their lives' never rings more true here. You and all the lads are and additive to society and I'm forever greatful to celebrate ball with you boys," a fan wrote .

"Know that a many folks appreciate your candor, and…and we can see when you know where the line is, you measure the worth of crossing it or feather the line. Stand strong, trust the gut. The gut digest, and you do a great job of digesting!" a person said .

McAfee said he remains focused on celebrating sports and bringing people together despite the challenges that have come with his public profile.

articles.title: Harmanpreet, Sukhjeet score braces as India beat China 5-2 at Asian Champions Trophy
articles.summary: Captain Harmanpreet Singh and forward Sukhjeet Singh struck twice each as India continued their winning run at the Asian Champions Trophy, defeating a
articles.body: Captain Harmanpreet Singh and forward Sukhjeet Singh struck twice each as India continued their winning run at the Asian Champions Trophy, defeating a spirited China 5-2 in front of the home crowd at the Olympian Surjit Singh Hockey Stadium on Thursday.India, who had opened their campaign with a commanding 13-0 win over Bangladesh, had to work harder against a youthful Chinese side but eventually secured their second consecutive victory. Harmanpreet converted two penalty corners, while Sukhjeet scored twice from open play. Jugraj Singh added the fifth goal with another successful set-piece conversion.China, despite their defeat, showed resilience and threatened India at different stages, with Peng Yang and Chongcong Chen scoring from penalty corners. However, the hosts' attacking quality and ability to capitalise on crucial opportunities proved decisive.Sukhjeet breaks the deadlock as China put up a fightIndia dominated possession and made repeated circle entries from the opening whistle but struggled to create clear-cut chances in the early stages. The breakthrough finally arrived in the 13th minute when Jugraj produced a superb scoop from deep to find Sukhjeet inside the Chinese circle. The forward controlled the ball brilliantly before lifting it over goalkeeper Huanyu Wu.China earned their first penalty corner in the 18th minute, but India's defence held firm. The hosts then won two successive penalty corners in the 20th minute, only for Harmanpreet to miss the target with his second attempt.The young Chinese side continued to frustrate India's attacks and drew level in the 26th minute. Peng Yang converted their second penalty corner with a drag-flick past goalkeeper Krishan Bahadur Pathak.India responded almost immediately. A minute later, Harmanpreet restored the hosts' lead with a powerful, low flick from their third penalty corner to make it 2-1.China earned two more penalty corners in the closing stages of the first half but failed to convert either, allowing India to carry a narrow advantage into the break.Harmanpreet, Sukhjeet extend India's leadIndia began the second half on the front foot, and Harmanpreet struck again in the 31st minute, converting another penalty corner with a grounded flick to give the hosts a 3-1 cushion.Three minutes later, Sukhjeet completed his brace. The forward finished off a pass from Aditya Arjun Lalage after the latter controlled an aerial ball from Harmanpreet near the halfway line.China refused to surrender and reduced the deficit in the 36th minute. Chongcong Chen converted their fourth penalty corner with a well-executed variation, bringing the score to 4-2 and keeping the visitors in contention.India continued to press for more goals. Jugraj saw one of his penalty-corner attempts saved by Wu, but the defender made amends in the 47th minute, unleashing a powerful, grounded flick from a set piece to restore India's three-goal advantage.The hosts earned another penalty corner two minutes before the final hooter, but Harmanpreet's effort was kept out by the Chinese goalkeeper. India, however, had done enough to seal a comfortable 5-2 victory.India face Japan nextThe win gives India a second successive victory in the tournament following their emphatic opening-day triumph over Bangladesh. articles.title: Travelers are tired of paying big bucks for basic hotels. A new hotel brand wants to shake things up.
articles.summary: There's a trend to make travel in the U.S. more affordable while still giving travelers what they actually want from a hotel experience. What might they have...
articles.body:
With a first location planned for Port Angeles, Wash., outside of Olympic National Park in 2027, the new hotel brand Bamboo is promising hikers and road trippers stylish, affordable accommodations — and an alternative to the rundown (and possibly overpriced) motel many people opt for out of necessity.

It's part of a growing trend to make travel in the United States more affordable while still giving travelers what they actually want from a hotel experience.

Bamboo's executive team includes individuals from the minimalist hotel chain CitizenM and, much like that company, it aims to give visitors a luxury-adjacent experience at a lower price point. Though its rooms will be roughly 200 square feet, smaller than the typical hotel room, they'll include a private bathroom and have amenities like a projector for watching streaming services, an espresso machine, a refrigerator, a Bluetooth speaker, blackout blinds, a safe and storage for clothing and luggage.

Founder Nicholas Curcio tells Yahoo Travel that the average Bamboo room will be "roughly $20 a night more than a traditional economy motel, and roughly $20 a night less than a Hampton Inn or Best Western."

(There are a few Best Westerns roughly two hours from Port Angeles, and a Hampton Inn about the same distance away. But travelers might look to the nearby Holiday Inn Express & Suites in Sequim, which is a similar tier, for an idea of nightly rates.)

It's meant to bridge the affordability-and-luxury gap not only by providing amenities guests actually want in their (smaller) rooms, but also by creating robust social spaces that encourage people to leave those rooms in the first place. Plans for the first property include a pizza oven, a movie-screening area and a fitness studio, plus a rooftop with a hot tub, sauna, cold plunge and elevated breakfast service. (Breakfast burritos with a view of the Olympic Mountains, anyone?)

Curcio saw a gap in the market in Port Angeles, and other destinations like it: The motels and hotels in the area were decades old, but some could still go for $400 a night — all for an experience that Curcio says could "leave guests feeling disappointed, or frankly, even unsafe."

And while Bamboo will target hikers who want to explore a national park but sleep in civilization, the intent isn't to stop there.

"Longer term, we believe the problem Bamboo is solving isn't unique to outdoor destinations," Curcio tells Yahoo Travel. "It's true across most of the U.S. lodging market: cool hotels are unaffordable, and affordable hotels are uncool. Over time, we aim for Bamboo to become the go-to off-highway brand, in the same category as a Best Western or Courtyard by Marriott, but one that feels far less corporate, delivers an experience built for this century and comes at a more accessible price point."

Bamboo isn't the only hotel brand seeking to change how people travel domestically. While international travel may involve costly flights, domestic travel — particularly when visiting big cities like New York City, Los Angeles or Washington, D.C. — comes with its own hefty price tag.

"If a traveler is attending a concert or an event, or they have to spend most of the time outside of their hotel, they don't really want to spend tons of money for the room," Vanja Bogicevic , a clinical associate professor of hospitality marketing at the NYU SPS Jonathan M. Tisch Center of Hospitality, tells Yahoo Travel. "But the real estate is such that the lower and more economy or mid-scale hotels don't have a place in a busy location."

Abroad, there's another answer — at least for the traveler who doesn't mind trading a bit of privacy and space for significantly cheaper accommodations. While hostels have long been popular in Europe and are particularly useful for solo travelers seeking to meet others in the cities they are visiting, capsule hotels have also popped up all across the globe.

First popularized in Osaka, Japan, in the 1970s , capsule hotels were originally a way for Japanese workers living outside the city to get some shut-eye before heading home.

While capsule hotel styles vary, what makes these hotels unique is that they offer travelers a place to sleep — but not much else. In some of these hotels, guests bed down in small, private capsules in larger rooms and share bathroom facilities with other guests. Now, these hotels are popping up in cities such as Copenhagen, Denmark; Zurich, Switzerland; Singapore; Cusco, Peru; and Bangkok, Thailand.

But the U.S. hasn't quite embraced the capsule hotel yet — and Bogicevic says American culture is one reason why.

"The American consumer [wants] more space and the culture is generally more expressive, and louder," she says. And in general, the American traveler prefers more privacy — meaning the shared bathroom experience isn't ideal.

If capsule hotels aren't the answer, however, more basic accommodations may be. While Bamboo may be the newest name on the market, chains like CitizenM, Moxy and Pod Hotel all offer smaller rooms and more basic amenities in major cities like New York in order to reduce the price of these hotels. While many chains like these feature private bathrooms, the emphasis is on keeping the rooms simple and making the common areas more appealing, with bars and other lounge areas for guests to utilize.

Chekitan S. Dev , a professor of hospitality management at Cornell University who serves on Bamboo's advisory board, tells Yahoo Travel that this new class of hotels can offer guests a taste of "affordable luxury" by focusing only on what they really want and cutting back in the areas less significant to the target demographic they're seeking to serve. This looks like using technology (think: self-check-in desks or vending machines for necessities), skipping a concierge desk and offering less frequent housekeeping services. Essentially, "extra frills that they don't need and don't want to pay for," he says.

Of course, not everyone will choose to stay at these types of hotels, even if they are more affordable. Dev says that when he and his wife stayed at one of these hotels in New York City, the tight room wasn't for them.

"It was too small," he says. "For a 60-something boomer, we're not in that target market."

articles.title: ‘I don’t think perfection exists, but I’m searching for it’: Kynan Chenai’s unfinished Olympic pursuit | TOISA Spotlight
articles.summary: “Goosebumps!” That is the first word Kynan Chenai uses when asked what comes to mind when he thinks back to the Asian Games mixed-team trap final.
articles.body: “Goosebumps!”That is the first word Kynan Chenai uses when asked what comes to mind when he thinks back to the Asian Games mixed-team trap final. He and Neeru Dhanda had won gold for India, but Chenai says there was little room to think about the medal while he was shooting.His attention was on the target, the gun mount, and the moment he needed to press the trigger. “At that point, nothing else mattered. It didn't matter if someone missed a target or if someone else broke theirs. All that mattered was hitting my target.” The emotion came later. “So, sitting here with you and thinking about it now, the one word that comes to mind is goosebumps.”Chenai had finished 16th in qualification in the individual event. In the mixed team, held a day later, he combined with Neeru Dhanda to qualify for the final and then shot 19 of 20 in the final. The change in performance was not lost on him.“At the Asian Games, I'm glad my experience and ability allowed me to flip the switch between the individual competition and the mixed-team event,” he says. “I was able to back myself and get that energy back after the individual event, which had taken place just a day earlier.”“I'm glad I was able to flip that switch. However, it comes down to my experience and my ability to grit my teeth and grind through difficult situations.”The final also required Chenai to work alongside Dhanda, who had come off a demanding Asian Games campaign and was exhausted after shooting in the rain. He says the two had their own routines and that he trusted her to know what she was doing.He told her he would help if she needed anything; otherwise, they would focus on their targets and assess the result afterwards. Dhanda told him at one point, “My battery is down.” Chenai's reply was characteristically brief: “Then go and recharge it!” He laughs about their banter and says he was impressed by how she found the energy to keep going.“Eventually, I was very impressed by how she managed to gather some energy and hold everything together to a certain extent. I'm glad I was able to do the same, and it worked out very well for the country.”The 38-year-old barrel behind the goldThere was another detail behind the performance: the barrel on his gun belonged to his father, Darius Chenai, former national trap champion, who introduced Kynan to the sport when he was 10. The barrel was 38 years old.Chenai had been using a high-rib barrel for four or five years but was not getting the consistency he wanted. The decision to change it came after discussions with his team. His Perazzi gun allows different components to be fitted to the same action, so he could use another barrel without changing the entire gun. He did not have a regular barrel at home; his father's gun was the only one with one available.“I asked him, and he said, ‘Yeah, take it, use it.’ He wasn't using it at the time.”The older barrel worked well enough to be part of an Asian Games gold-medal performance.His father has since been teasing him about how many shells he is putting through it and warning him to be careful with something already so old. “But at the end of the day, it's all fun and jokes with him. He's quite proud that I've been able to use something of his and achieve some success with it.”The first person who taught him to shootDarius was also the person who first took Chenai to the range and put a gun in his hands. A two-time national champion in trap shooting, he taught his son the basics of shooting and, just as importantly, how to handle a firearm safely.Chenai says his father explained that a gun had to be respected, cleaned and put away properly. Some of the techniques he learnt then remain part of his shooting today.“I've had many different role models throughout my career. I could give you a list of names, but Dad is one of them. He's the first one, the OG.”He also names Manjir Singh, Manojit Singh Sandhu and Ranjan Sodhi as influences. More recently, David Kostelecki, his coach and a two-time Olympic medallist, has become an important source of advice. “I've been trying to learn from him how to win an Olympic medal. I keep picking his brain.”Chenai grew up in Hyderabad and spent 10 years at Hebron School in Ooty. He describes himself as a child more interested in sport than studies, keen to be involved in whatever was happening around him.Prithviraj Tondaiman, an accomplished Indian trap shooter who competed at the Paris 2024 Olympics and was part of India's gold-medal-winning men's trap team at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, was a young shooter at the range when Chenai was growing up. Tondaiman has often told him that he wanted to do everything: put the microphone on the range, load clay targets into the machine, check that it worked, shoot and then pick up the empty cartridges.“I was one of those kids who wanted to be involved in everything,” Chenai says. “I was into hockey, swimming, shooting and football. I loved everything.” Eventually, he had to settle on one sport. “But eventually, as life goes on, you realise that you don't have enough time to do everything. You have to pick one thing, and I'm glad I picked this one.”Rio, the missed Olympics and the road to LAThe Olympics became the main target in his twenties. Chenai was 25 when he made his debut at Rio 2016, but he now looks back at that version of himself as a shooter who wanted to reach the Games without fully understanding what it took to win a medal there.“In my twenties, the one goal was to go to the Olympics. That was the main thing I wanted to achieve. However, I didn't know how to win an Olympic medal. I was a kid running on fumes. I was just shooting my way through whatever I could, relying on sheer grit and, as they say, sheer dumb luck.”Rio gave him the experience of competing at the Olympics and, in his words, a clearer sense of what he needed to do differently next time. Chenai finished 19th in the men's trap qualification with a score of 114. “That was a great experience for me because I learnt what to do and what not to do for my next Olympics. It was as simple as that.”He missed Tokyo and then Paris, both disappointments for a shooter who still wants another Olympic opportunity. But Chenai says he has learnt to move on rather than let the absence consume the next phase of his career.“I still have the goal of going to the Olympics. Yes, as you said, I missed the last two, which was disappointing, but it wasn't earth-shattering. I had already been to the Olympics in Rio.”However, the disappointment does not vanish while the Games are under way. He watches other athletes compete and thinks about being there himself.“When the Olympic fever is at its peak, you're watching the Games on TV and seeing people do great things. You want to be part of it too, right? When you're not there, it hurts.” His own measure of time is the closing ceremony. “But after the closing ceremony, you move on and carry on.”Getting to Los Angeles, one competition at a timeLos Angeles 2028 is the next Olympic target, but Chenai is not looking to plan every step two years in advance. He wants to win another World Cup medal, too, and says his focus has shifted towards the competition immediately in front of him.Asked how he is approaching the final stretch towards LA, he answers without dressing it up: “There's no thinking behind it. There's just winning.” The first task is to win a quota place for India. He says that can be done at a World Cup, World Championship or Asian Championship, after which an athlete must qualify through trials in India under the federation's selection policy.“Without a quota place, we can't go. So, it comes back to what I was telling you earlier: give 100 per cent in one competition and see what happens. After that, we move on to the next one.”For Chenai, preparation means knowing when not to keep shooting. He says athletes can exhaust themselves mentally if they train hard right up to the competition. A shooter might put in 200 shells a day for 10 days, only to arrive at the event tired of repeating the same routine.“You're going to make a mistake, almost certainly, because you've been training with 200 shells a day for the last 10 days. You'll come back the next day, and your mind will say, ‘Oh man, we've got to do this again?’”His team follows a regimented tapering process to make sure he is mentally fresh when it counts. The rest of life has to be kept under control, too.“You also work very hard to make sure everything in your life settles down around the time of your competition. After the competition, things can become hectic again. But during that period, your life has to be very mellow. There should be no drama, nothing.” He describes it as work that happens away from the trigger.Balancing life beyond the shooting rangeHe has also had to make room for life outside the range. Chenai got married seven months before and his businesses take up time as well.“I'm 35 now, so, as my family says, it's high time!” he says. “Shooting is my one love, of course, it takes up a lot of our time and effort.”“However, life has changed between my twenties and my thirties. I have to give time to other things in life as well. I have to make time for my family, my businesses and whatever else there is outside shooting.”He says the balance has changed his appreciation for the hours he gets at the range: “When I'm on the range, my appreciation for the game is greater because I love it so much and value the time I get to do what I need to do.”Chenai has been part of Indian shooting long enough to see changes in the support available to athletes. He credits National Rifle Association of India president Raninder Singh with helping put systems in place through which shooters can train at NCOEs, receive support under the Target Olympic Podium Scheme and access ammunition regularly.“He's put standard operating procedures in place that allow athletes to be part of NCOE and TOPS, receive ammunition and practise their targets every day. Not every month, but every day.” In his view, the ability to train consistently for around 250 days a year helps shooters develop the muscle memory needed to compete internationally.He says India's shotgun shooters have made progress, while rifle and pistol shooters remain capable of competing with the best despite a disappointing Asian Games. “Okay, they didn't have a good Asian Games. So what? In my opinion, they are still the best in the world. Indian rifle and pistol shooters are among the top performers. Shotgun is coming along, and you've seen that here.”He is also quick to point out that each discipline comes with different demands. Shotgun takes place outdoors, where rain and sun can affect competition; indoor shooters deal with conditions such as temperature and lighting. “I don't know all the logistics involved, but I can tell you that every sport has its own difficulties, and we are genuine contenders at the world level.”Still searching for perfectionChenai does not claim to have worked everything out. He says the years since Hangzhou have made him more mature in how he responds to competition, and that handling pressure remains a learning process.“I'm not saying I'm perfect or that I've figured everything out, because that's not possible. Nobody does that. I say this all the time: I don't think perfection exists, but I'm searching for it.”Asked what success means to him now, he does not reduce it to a medal count or an Olympic appearance. “It's about being the best version of myself, yes. And I can also tell you that if I'm consistent, I'm successful.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Van Mathias bate un récord mundial y rescata el mito del bigote mágico de Spitz
articles.standfirst: El americano rebaja la plusmarca de los 100 braza y Kate Douglass iguala el de los 50 libre
articles.summary: El americano rebaja la plusmarca de los 100 braza y Kate Douglass iguala el de los 50 libre
articles.body: La segunda jornada de los Trials estadounidenses de piscina corta en Westmont (Illinois) arrojó un récord del mundo que rescata uno de los episodios más hilarantes de la historia de la natación, el deporte de los cuerpos depilados por obligación de la aerodinámica. Van Mathias, de 2000, nadador forjado en la universidad de Indiana y con el bigote como distintivo, batió el récord del mundo de 100 braza que tenía el bielorruso Ilya Shymanovich desde 2021. El estadounidense nadó los cuatro largos en 55.14, catorce centésimas más rápido que su antecesor, para arrojar el primer récord mundial de su vida, algo también poco frecuente en la natación que a sus plusmarquistas los estrena a menor edad. Es su mostacho lo que evoca otros figuras inolvidables de otros nadadores históricos que también lo lucieron como Matt Biondi (ocho oros entre Seúl'88 y Barcelona'92), John Naber, el autor de cuatro oros con otros tantos récords mundiales en los Juegos de Montreal 76 y, sobre todo, Mark Spitz, el nadador que había protagonizado la mayor hazaña de la historia de este deporte en Munich 1972 con siete oros hasta la exhibición de Michael Phelps en Pekín 2008. Spitz dejó crecer pelo debajo de su nariz por un acto de rebeldía frente a un entrenador que le aconsejó que se lo afeitase, pero cuando antes del comienzo de la cita muniquesa barruntaba hacerlo sucedió un hecho que cambió su idea. En plena guerra fría con la Unión Soviética, el versátil nadador fue a entrenarse y los técnicos soviéticos se arremolinaron en torno a su calle. Al salir, le preguntaron sobre las razones por las que lucía ese bigote. —Este bigote desvía el agua de mi boca —dijo con total seriedad—. Me hace más hidrodinámico y me ayuda a nadar más rápido. Los soviéticos creyeron esa teoría y al año siguiente aparecieron en los Mundiales de Belgrado todos sus nadadores con él, aunque su resultado fue pobre: no ganaron ninguna medalla de oro y sólo Mikhail Khryukin arrancó una plata. Mientras, en el sector femenino de la velocidad, Kate Douglass sigue con su singular duelo con su compañera de entrenamientos en Virginia, Gretchen Walsh. Volvió a batirla en los 50 libre e igualó el récord del mundo que su amiga (27.55) había instaurado hace un par de semanas. El duelo entre ambas, también escenificado en la piscina de 50 metros, está llevando la disciplina más rápida de la natación a otro nivel. Además, Caeleb Dressel, el que revolucionó los Juegos de Tokio en 2021, nadó muy rápido los 100 estilos. Lo hizo en 50.34, récord de los campeonatos, aunque lejos del mundial que él posee desde 2020 (49.28). Nada mal para una prueba que sólo había nadado previamente una vez en los últimos cinco años.

articles.summary: India will have a 17-member contingent, featuring 11 women and six men, competing across 11 sports at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Senegal from
articles.body: India will have a 17-member contingent, featuring 11 women and six men, competing across 11 sports at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Senegal from October 31 to November 13.Table tennis player Syndrela Das, badminton talent Tanvi Patri and swimmer Dhinidhi Desinghu are among the country's leading medal prospects at the fourth edition of the Summer Youth Olympics, which will be staged in Africa for the first time.Das will take part in the women's singles table tennis competition, while Asian Under-17 badminton champion Patri will represent India in the women's singles event. Desinghu is entered in three swimming events: the women's 100m freestyle, 200m freestyle and 200m individual medley.India's participation will span athletics, archery, badminton, beach wrestling, boxing, equestrian, judo, swimming, table tennis, windsurfing and wushu. The 17-athlete squad will be the country's smallest contingent at a Summer Youth Olympic Games.The 2026 edition will be held across Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly over 15 days. Around 2,700 athletes are expected to compete in 25 sports for 153 medal events. Ten additional engagement sports will also be part of the programme, but will not offer medals.Dakar 2026 will mark the first time an Olympic sporting event is held on African soil. The Games were initially scheduled for 2022 but were postponed by four years due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The previous Summer Youth Olympics took place in Buenos Aires, Argentina, in 2018.India have collected 23 medals across the three previous editions, comprising three gold, 16 silver and four bronze. The inaugural Games were held in Singapore in 2010, followed by Nanjing in China in 2014 and Buenos Aires in 2018.Organised by the International Olympic Committee (IOC), the Youth Olympic Games are designed for athletes primarily aged between 15 and 17. Alongside sporting competition, the event features educational and cultural programmes aimed at promoting Olympic values, participation and international understanding.The 2026 sports programme includes athletics, swimming, breaking, skateboarding, beach handball, beach wrestling, futsal, coastal rowing, Baseball5 and Wushu Taolu, among others. Baseball5 and Wushu Taolu will make their Youth Olympic Games debut. articles.title: Kenya’s 2029 World Athletics bid: A win for Africa under scrutiny
articles.summary: Kenya aims to turn its rich athletics heritage into a lasting legacy for the continent.
articles.body:
Nairobi, Kenya – For more than four decades, the World Athletics Championships have been held across continents but never in Africa.

That changes in 2029, when Nairobi becomes the first African city to host the track and field championships, bringing the sport’s flagship global competition to a continent whose athletes have helped shape its history.

The World Athletics Championships were established in 1983 in Helsinki, Finland, after decades in which athletics’ biggest global competitions were largely tied to the Olympic Games. The inaugural championships brought together 1,333 athletes from 153 countries, laying the foundation for one of the most important events on the international sporting calendar.

Africa’s relationship with athletics stretches much further back. Ethiopia’s Abebe Bikila became the first African to win Olympic marathon gold in 1960, followed by generations of track and field athletes including Uganda’s John Akii-Bua, Morocco’s Said Aouita and a succession of Kenyan champions.

Kenya’s own story is particularly significant. Kipchoge Keino’s 1,500-metre triumph at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics helped establish Kenya as a global distance-running powerhouse. Generations that followed – from Paul Tergat and David Rudisha to Eliud Kipchoge, Vivian Cheruiyot, Hellen Obiri and Faith Kipyegon – have turned Kenyan athletics into a global sporting identity.

Kenya is the second most successful nation in World Athletics Championships history.

For Keino, the two-time Olympic champion and former world record holder whose achievements helped establish Kenya’s reputation in distance running, Nairobi’s selection represents the culmination of decades of progress.

“When we started running, we were young Kenyans with a dream to represent our country and show the world that African athletes could compete at the highest level. Seeing Kenya prepare to host the World Athletics Championships in 2029 is a deeply special moment,” Keino told Al Jazeera.

“It is a testament to how far our country has come from sending athletes abroad to compete, to welcoming the world to our own home.”

Keino said hosting the championships would also give Kenya an opportunity to showcase its talent, culture and hospitality while investing in the future of athletics.

Kenya’s campaign to host the 2029 championships lasted three years and culminated in victory at the World Athletics Council meeting in Budapest on September 15 .

Competing bids came from London, Rome and Munich, all cities with established records of hosting major international athletics events.

Nairobi’s bid highlighted the ongoing renovation of Kasarani stadium ahead of the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations , as well as Kenya’s experience hosting the 2017 World U18 Championships and the 2021 World U20 junior Championships. Kenya also drew lessons from its unsuccessful bid for the 2025 championships, which was awarded to Tokyo.

World Athletics President Sebastian Coe said the council had received four strong bids and described Nairobi’s proposal as “compelling and emotional”.

“Nairobi and Munich ultimately presented two compelling propositions. They offer very different but equally exciting opportunities for our sport, and I am delighted that we can now begin working with both cities to stage two world-class championships,” Coe said.

Athletics Kenya declined to comment on the decision.

The celebrations were quickly accompanied by questions over whether Kenya can host an event of this scale while dealing with persistent scrutiny over doping in athletics.

Since the international sport governing body World Athletics established the Athletics Integrity Unit in 2017, 318 Kenyan athletes have been sanctioned for anti-doping rule violations, according to figures reported following the announcement. Of those, 136 were still serving bans.

Kenya is not among the countries with the highest overall number of anti-doping violations globally, but its prominence in distance running means high-profile cases often attract considerable international attention.

Kenya’s anti-doping system has also faced scrutiny. In 2025, the World Anti-Doping Agency found Kenya’s anti-doping agency non-compliant with the global anti-doping code, putting additional scrutiny on the country’s system. Kenya was removed from the agency’s compliance watchlist in 2026 after corrective measures.

Recent cases, including the bans of marathon world-record holder Ruth Chepngetich and former half-marathon world-record holder Kibiwott Kandie, have kept the issue in the spotlight.

For Nairobi, the challenge will be to demonstrate that its anti-doping systems are strong enough to protect the credibility of the 2029 championships.

Kenyan Member of Parliament Dan Wanyama, who chairs the committee on sports and culture, said the country has the experience and infrastructure to host the event.

“We have already held several athletics championships which were very successful. It is a thing of pride for us to defeat major global cities London, Munich and Rome,” Wanyama told Al Jazeera.

“As the chair of the sports committee in Parliament, I can assure you we have the right infrastructure in place because the championship will be held at Moi International Sports Stadium (known locally as Kasarani). The contractor is already on site and preparations have started in earnest.”

Kenyan athletics fan Winston Omondi said some of the criticism of Kenya was unfairly focused on the country.

“If it was about doping, then there are so many developed countries that should not even be participating in athletics, including London itself,” Omondi told Al Jazeera.

Doping is not the only test facing Kenya.

As the country prepares to host the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations with sporting infrastructure being upgraded at Kasarani and Nyayo stadiums, the World Athletics Championships will require more than a competition venue.

Nairobi will have to ensure adequate training and warm-up facilities while improving transport links, accommodation and athlete services. The city will also need reliable systems for security, accreditation, broadcasting, medical care and the movement of thousands of athletes, officials, journalists and spectators.

Beyond the stadiums, Nairobi’s wider infrastructure will come under scrutiny, particularly its traffic congestion and public transport network.

The success of the championships will therefore depend on more than upgrading Kasarani. Kenya will have to demonstrate that Nairobi can deliver a seamless experience for a global sporting event while maintaining the standards expected of one of athletics’ biggest competitions.

For a country whose athletes have spent decades representing Africa on the world stage, hosting the championships is a historic opportunity. It is also a test of whether a continent that has produced generations of world-class athletes can host the sport’s biggest global events on its own ground.

But winning the bid was only the first race.

As Omondi put it: “We have come so far as people, as a country and as a continent for us to be judged in this way.”

articles.title: Mark Stewart: Cyclist's rise from lifeguard to world champion
articles.summary: Scotland's Mark Stewart stopped cycling professionally after the Covid-19 pandemic. Now he is a world champion in the points race at age 31.
articles.body:
Scotland's Mark Stewart admits he had started to accept he would never win a gold medal at the World Track Cycling Championships - before he finally became world champion in China earlier this month.

The 31-year-old, who had previously claimed two silver medals and a bronze, prevailed in the gruelling 160-lap points race in Shanghai to reach the pinnacle of his career.

Stewart, from Dundee, was dropped by British Cycling's high performance programme and stopped cycling professionally after the Covid-19 pandemic hit.

After being stranded in New Zealand during lockdown he stayed in the country and had to make a living away from sport, working as a dog walker, babysitter, teacher, and lifeguard before rejoining British Cycling before the 2024 Olympics.

Stewart admits his rise at a later stage in his career has left him unsure about how to process his world-title success.

"Because it had taken me so long to win a world championship you almost start to make your peace that it wasn't going to happen and started to enjoy the other aspects of sport," Stewart told BBC Scotland.

"I don't put any more value on it because I have spent my career telling myself that it is not where I put my value, so I can't see that really changing.

"I stand by that so I think it is something cool and it is a personal achievement - but I still don't think it should change how people judge you or how I judge myself."

Stewart and Morris add to GB gold tally at Worlds

Stewart admits he had to overcome some "extremely challenging" personal circumstances in the build up to his victory, which he says he was able to "channel" into his performance.

After getting a taste of Olympic action in Paris two years ago, the 2018 Commonwealth gold medallist believes he can tap into his experience and fresh heights to compete at the next Olympics in Los Angeles in 2028.

"That world championships was the start of the Olympic selection process so I couldn't really have started it in a better place," he said.

"I have found a new level of performance and I think if I can tap into that it might open up a few more doors, I might still have to push the doors but a re-evaluation probably is needed."

articles.title: ‘Injury much better now’: Neeraj Chopra on the path to recovery; to resume training and rehabilitation in next few weeks
articles.summary: New Delhi: Olympic and world champion javelin thrower Neeraj Chopra said his recovery from injury is on the right path and training, rehab process will
articles.body: New Delhi: Olympic and world champion javelin thrower Neeraj Chopra said his recovery from injury is on the right path and training, rehab process will begun in the next couple of weeks. The 2020 Tokyo Olympics gold medallist has kept next year as his target after sustaining an injury, with his focus on delivering strong performances ahead of LA 2028.Chopra, who won gold at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics and silver at the Paris 2024 Olympics in men's javelin throw, has been one of India's leading figures in recent years. However, Chopra missed the recent 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya after he suffered an ankle ligament injury during a training session, which also ruled him out for the rest of the season."My injury is much better now. I faced some issues initially in the first month and a half, but it has improved significantly. I consulted Dr. Dinshaw Pardiwala and he has advised that I can now resume training and begin proper rehabilitation. My plan is to start both in the next couple of weeks," Neeraj told SAI Media.The two-time Olympic medallist clarified that he followed complete rest as advised by his medical team."For my injury, the doctors had advised rest, and that is exactly what I followed. With regard to competitions, TOPS (Target Olympic Podium Scheme) and SAI (Sports Authority of India) have been supporting me for years. I have been part of the TOPS Core Group for many years now, and whenever I need any support, they are there," he added.In Neeraj and Kishore Jena's absence, Yashvir Singh won a silver medal and Rohit Yadav a bronze in javelin throw at the 2026 Asian Games.Neeraj also welcomed the Union Cabinet's approval of the Khelo India Sports Goods Manufacturing Scheme on October 28, calling it a major step for Indian sport."The Khelo India Sports Goods Manufacturing Scheme, which was approved by the Union Cabinet, is an amazing step. Athletes face a lot of issues in procuring certain equipment in India or have to import sporting equipment from abroad. With schemes like these, as equipment will be manufactured in India, it will become much easier for them to source it," he noted.He then went on to extend his best wishes to the Indian contingent for the upcoming Youth Olympic Games and added, "I wish all the best to the athletes heading to the Youth Olympics. Enjoy the experience and don't take too much pressure or get nervous. Whatever pressure you face at the Youth Olympics is good for you as it teaches you a lot. Use this opportunity to observe others and channel the pressure to your advantage, and I am sure you will do your best."Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Cas overturns ban on Russia by ice hockey's global governing body
articles.summary: The Court of Arbitration for Sport overturns the ban on Russia by ice hockey's global governing body.
articles.body:
The Court of Arbitration for Sport has overturned the ban on Russia by ice hockey's global governing body.

Russia have been suspended from competing in International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) events since the country invaded Ukraine in February 2022.

Earlier this year the IIHF said Russia's teams would remain excluded after a review by the organisation's council.

The Russian Ice Hockey Federation (RIHF) appealed that decision to Cas, which has upheld it following an in-person hearing at its headquarters in Lausanne, Switzerland.

A statement from Cas , external said that arguments made by the IIHF "citing safety, security and other concerns" were "not supported by sufficient evidence".

Russia are now set to be part of IIHF events in the 2026-27 season, including the men's and women's World Championships.

It is unclear what restrictions, if any, will be in place in relation to flags, clothing and the playing of the national anthem.

Individual athletes from Russia were allowed to compete at the 2026 Winter Olympics in Italy under a neutral flag, although not in ice hockey.

"The IIHF disagrees with this aspect of the ruling and maintains that its decisions were necessary to protect the safety and security of all participants and safeguard the integrity of its competitions," they said in a statement.

"While the IIHF respects the authority of Cas and will act in accordance with its ruling, the outcome does not remove the concerns that informed its assessments."

Ukraine have qualified for next year's men's World Championship, which is scheduled to be held in Germany from 14 to 30 May.

The IIHF said the ruling has not taken into account the material impact of the decision including a review of competition formats, schedules, travel and accommodation arrangements, and safety and security measures.

"Cas does not consider the practical elements which cannot be implemented immediately," it added.

"Changes to participation require extensive coordination with the relevant Member National Associations, organising committees and host authorities."

A statement from the RIHF said it "welcomes the decision" from Cas and they will work with the IIHF to "facilitate the return of Russian teams to competitions".

articles.title: Asian Champions Trophy Hockey: Abhishek's brace powers India to 4-1 win over Japan
articles.summary: India continued their winning run in the men's Asian Champions Trophy hockey tournament with a convincing 4-1 victory over Japan on Friday.
articles.body: India continued their winning run in the men's Asian Champions Trophy hockey tournament with a convincing 4-1 victory over Japan on Friday. Striker Abhishek Nain scored twice as the five-time champions registered their third consecutive win in the tournament.India had started their campaign with a 13-0 win over Bangladesh before beating China 5-2. Japan, meanwhile, had defeated South Korea 3-2 and Bangladesh 1-0 in their first two matches.Abhishek (11th, 51st minutes) scored two field goals, while captain Harmanpreet Singh (47th) converted India's only penalty corner of the match. Vishnukant Singh (56th) also scored a field goal.Shota Yamada (15th) scored Japan's only goal through a penalty stroke.Asian Games champions India will next take on Malaysia on Sunday. India had defeated Malaysia 5-1 at the recent Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. Japan will face China in their next match.Abhishek gives India the lead, Japan hit backJapan started the match with more possession and put early pressure on the Indian defence. They earned a penalty corner in the second minute, but Ken Nagayoshi's attempt from a variation went wide.India took some time to settle into the match. There was a lack of coordination between the midfield and forward line, with vice-captain Hardik Singh doing most of the work without much support.With Mandeep Singh missing the match, the Indian forwards also struggled to create clear scoring chances.However, India broke the deadlock in the 11th minute through a well-worked field goal.Hardik started the move and found Sukhjeet Singh inside the circle near the left corner. Sukhjeet then passed the ball to Abhishek, who was playing his 150th international match. Abhishek made no mistake and guided the ball into the goal to give India a 1-0 lead.Japan responded by earning another penalty corner, but their attempt went wide.They continued to put pressure on India and earned two more penalty corners in the final seconds of the first quarter. The second attempt led to a penalty stroke after the ball hit Sanjay's body. Shota Yamada converted it past Indian goalkeeper Suraj Karkera to make it 1-1.Japan's defence keeps India quietJapan defended in numbers and made it difficult for the Indian attackers to find space inside the circle.Their man-to-man marking was effective, and India struggled to create clear chances. The teams went into the half-time break with the scores level at 1-1.India did not win a single penalty corner in the first half.Three minutes into the third quarter, Hardik created a good chance for Sukhjeet, but the forward's shot from inside the circle went over the goal.Japan continued to play well and earned their fourth penalty corner in the 36th minute. However, captain Raiki Fujishima's flick went over the post.India also came close to scoring when Shilanand Lakra tried a reverse hit after receiving a defence-splitting pass from Amit Rohidas. But Japanese goalkeeper Takumi Kitagawa made the save.Harmanpreet, Abhishek and Vishnukant seal India's winWith the scores still level at 1-1 after three quarters, India stepped up their attack in the final 15 minutes.The hosts earned their first penalty corner of the match in the 46th minute. Captain Harmanpreet Singh made the opportunity count with a powerful low flick to put India ahead 2-1.The goal gave India some breathing room, and the forwards began putting Japan's defence under constant pressure.Abhishek scored his second goal of the match in the 51st minute after another good attacking move, extending India's lead to 3-1.Vishnukant Singh then added another goal four minutes before the final hooter. He received a perfectly placed aerial pass from Harmanpreet and finished the move to make it 4-1.India held on to their three-goal advantage to register their third straight victory in the tournament.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Hellen Obiri ready to defend NYC Marathon title on path to L.A. Games
articles.summary: Hellen Obiri is a two-time New York City Marathon winner looking for her third title as she chases another goal: elusive Olympic marathon gold.
articles.body:
After four consecutive years competing in the New York City Marathon, including wins in 2023 and 2025, Hellen Obiri knows the course like the back of her hand.

But as the 36-year-old Kenyan champion prepares to defend her NYC Marathon title on Sunday, Nov. 1, she knows familiarity and confidence alone won't guarantee the result.

"It's a marathon. You can't underrate anybody and anybody can win," Obiri told USA TODAY Sports. "So for me, what I have right now is pressure."

Obiri, who played netball in Kenya before deciding to pursue running, is the only woman to win world titles in indoor track, outdoor track and cross country. She started her career competing in the 800, the 1,500, the 5,000 and 10,000 meters. But Obiri said she always wondered how far her body could go.

In 2022, Obiri joined Swiss sportswear brand On's Athletic Training Club and moved to Boulder, Colorado, to train with Dathan Ritzenhein. That same year, Obiri made her marathon debut in New York City, placing sixth. She won the race in 2023, finished as runner-up in 2024, and set a new course record (02:19:51) while capturing her second title in 2025.

Although she relishes her NYC Marathon titles, Obiri also has her sights set on a different achievement: winning Olympic gold at the 2028 Games in Los Angeles. She made her Olympic debut for Kenya in 2012, won Olympic silver medals in the 5,000 at the 2016 and 2021 Games, then won bronze in the marathon at the 2024 Paris Games.

If Obiri qualifies for the 2028 Games, it will be her fifth Olympics.

"Winning the Olympics will be a lifetime title," Obiri said. "I can say somebody won the Olympics in 1984. When somebody (asks) you who won a major marathon in 1984, sometimes you have to go into Google and see who won. So I think if you have won everything, the major marathons, and you are missing the Olympic title, the Olympic title will be much more precious to you."

These celebrities are expected to run the 2026 New York City Marathon

Kenya will send a maximum of three women's marathon runners to the 2028 Olympics and qualification is not a given. Obiri said winning a major marathon in 2027 is paramount to making the Olympic team. This year's NYC Marathon will help gauge her fitness level and guide her training program for the next year.

Right now, Obiri is focused on staying healthy and balancing her running career with being a mother to her 11-year-old daughter.

"Apart from being an athlete, I have another big role to play out here," Obiri said. "When you go to the track, when you are training, you are an athlete. But when you come home, your family needs you. Your daughter needs you."

Obiri said the New York marathon is like her "second home," but described it as the toughest course of the major marathons with its difficult corners and hills. Given how familiar Obiri is with the course, her biggest challenge is not to let her mind outpace her feet.

"I have that course in my mind. From mile one to mile 26, I know everything that will happen right away," Obiri said. "You can't say, 'I need to think about winning,' or, 'I need to think about mile 24.' Every step I take one mile at a time."
